\chapter{Gente Y Trato}
\label{ch:es-gente}
\hlchaptermodality{436}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about colleagues and groups, offer an alternative, and say who lent, collected or returned a thing.}

Read the notice or advert this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el compañero]{el compañero — you already know where this comes from}

\label{lesson:ES-C436-companero}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el pan}. When you learned it you were told what \emph{com-} plus \emph{pānis} makes. Say that word now, before reading on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el compañero}
\textbf{el compañero / la compañera} — the colleague, the classmate, the companion.

\textbf{You were given the etymology long ago and never the word.} The bread lesson told you it means \emph{one you share bread with}; this lesson hands you the word to use.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{com-} with, plus \textbf{pan}, bread, plus \textbf{-ero}, the person-ending you met on \emph{la portera}. Three pieces you already hold, and not one of them new.

What is worth adding is how wide the word runs in practice:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{phrase} & \textbf{who it means} \\
\midrule
un compañero de trabajo & a colleague \\
un compañero de clase & a classmate \\
mi compañero & a partner, depending on context \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

On its own, \textbf{mi compañero} is ambiguous between a work partner and a life partner, and Spanish speakers disambiguate with \emph{de trabajo}, \emph{de piso}, \emph{de clase} when it matters. That ambiguity is not sloppiness; the word never promised more than \emph{the one I share things with}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el compañero}
  \item a colleague from work
  \item the three pieces the word is made of
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The colleague? (\textbf{el compañero}.) What is hiding in the middle of it? (\textbf{pan}.) How do you make it mean \emph{classmate}? (\textbf{de clase}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el grupo]{el grupo — the unit things get organised into}

\label{lesson:ES-C436-grupo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la clase}. Say \emph{el compañero}. A course splits its people into smaller sets. Name a set.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el grupo}
\textbf{el grupo} — the group.

\textbf{cambiar de grupo} — to switch groups. \textbf{el grupo de los martes} — the Tuesday group.

\begin{cousinweb}
This one does not come apart. It arrived whole, by way of Italian, and there is no Spanish piece inside it to recognise.

That is the second thing this run has taught you about long-versus-short words:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{kind of word} & \textbf{what to do} \\
\midrule
long and formal & look for the ending \\
short and plain & learn it whole \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{el grupo} is short and plain, so there is nothing to unfold. Spending time hunting for a join in a five-letter noun is the opposite of the habit — the habit is to look \textbf{once}, cheaply, and move on when nothing is there.

Where it matters most for you is administrative: courses, trips, exams and sports are all divided into \emph{grupos}, and the DELE pass rule itself is written in terms of two of them.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el grupo}
  \item I have changed groups
  \item the Tuesday group is too advanced for me
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The group? (\textbf{el grupo}.) Does it come apart? (\textbf{No} — it arrived whole.) To switch groups? (\textbf{cambiar de grupo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ofrecer]{ofrecer — to carry it toward somebody}

\label{lesson:ES-C436-ofrecer}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{ayudar}. Say \emph{cobrar}. The restaurant has no table on Friday. Say what it does next instead of refusing outright.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ofrecer}
\textbf{ofrecer} — to offer.

\emph{Le puedo ofrecer el jueves} — I can offer you Thursday. It is the polite move between \emph{no} and nothing.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ob-} toward, plus \textbf{ferre}, to carry. To carry a thing toward somebody.

That \emph{ferre} is one of the most productive roots in the language, and once you see it you will read words you have never met:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{what is carried} \\
\midrule
ofrecer & toward you \\
transferir & across \\
referir & back \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Watch the spelling in the yo form.} \emph{Ofrecer} takes a \textbf{z} before the \emph{o}: \emph{ofrezco}, not \emph{ofreco}. Every verb ending \textbf{-cer} after a vowel does the same — \emph{conocer / conozco}, \emph{parecer / parezco} — so learning this one buys the pattern for a large family.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ofrecer}
  \item I can offer you Thursday
  \item the yo form, with its z
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To offer? (\textbf{ofrecer}.) The yo form? (\textbf{ofrezco}.) What do the two pieces mean? (\textbf{To carry toward}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[prestar]{prestar — the move that devolver undoes}

\label{lesson:ES-C436-prestar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{devolver}. Say \emph{el cargador}. You can already say you gave the charger back. Say how it reached you in the first place.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: prestar}
\textbf{prestar} — to lend.

\emph{Te presto el cargador} — I lend you the charger. And then, later, \emph{te lo devuelvo}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which way is it moving}]
English has one word doing two opposite jobs — people say \emph{borrow} and \emph{lend} and then muddle them. Spanish keeps the giver's side and marks the receiver's with a preposition:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
te presto el libro & I lend you the book \\
pedir prestado un libro & to borrow a book \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \textbf{prestar} is always the \textbf{lender} speaking. To be the borrower you say \emph{pedir prestado} — literally \emph{to ask for it lent}, which uses the \emph{pedir} under \textbf{el pedido} from four chapters ago.

The three verbs now sit in a cycle you can say end to end: \textbf{prestar} hands it over, the other person has it, \textbf{devolver} brings it back.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{prestar}
  \item I lend you my charger
  \item I lent it to him and he has not given it back
  \item how to say it from the borrower's side
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To lend? (\textbf{prestar}.) To borrow? (\textbf{pedir prestado}.) And to give it back? (\textbf{devolver}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[recoger]{recoger — to gather it back up}

\label{lesson:ES-C436-recoger}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el pedido}. Say \emph{el taller}. The order is ready and the car is repaired. Say what you go and do at both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: recoger}
\textbf{recoger} — to collect, to pick up, to fetch, to tidy away.

\emph{Vengo a recoger unas fotos} — I have come to collect some photos. \emph{Recojo a los niños del colegio} — I pick the children up from school.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{re-} back, plus \textbf{coger}, to take. To take back up what is there.

One Spanish verb covers what English splits four ways, and the split is arbitrary in English rather than meaningful:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you recoger} & \textbf{English wants} \\
\midrule
un pedido & collect \\
a los niños & pick up \\
la mesa & clear \\
la ropa tendida & bring in \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Hold the Spanish idea — \emph{gather back up} — and all four fall out of it. Trying to remember four English translations is four times the work for less accuracy.

\textbf{Watch the spelling}: \emph{recojo} with a \textbf{j} in the yo form, because \emph{ge} would be said differently from \emph{go}. The sound stays put and the letter moves, which is the reverse of what English spelling usually does to you.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{recoger}
  \item I have come to collect the order
  \item I pick the children up at five
  \item the yo form, with its j
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To collect? (\textbf{recoger}.) The yo form? (\textbf{recojo}.) What do the two pieces mean? (\textbf{To take back up}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(compañero, grupo, ofrecer, prestar …]{(compañero, grupo, ofrecer, prestar, recoger) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R436-repaso-gente}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{the colleague}, \emph{to lend} and \emph{to collect}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the cycle is now complete}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{step} & \textbf{verb} \\
\midrule
I hand it over & \textbf{presto} \\
you go and get it & \textbf{recoges} \\
you give it back & \textbf{devuelves} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six chapters ago you could buy a thing and pay for it. You can now describe its whole life: ordered, delayed, collected, lent, returned.

\textbf{prestar} is the lender's verb only. The borrower says \textbf{pedir prestado}, which contains the \emph{pedir} under \textbf{el pedido} from the first chapter of this run — so the cycle closes on the word it opened with.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{Two of these you could have guessed and did not need to be told.} \textbf{compañero} was fully explained when you learned \emph{pan}, years of pages ago in book time — \emph{com-} plus \emph{pānis}, one you share bread with — and all this chapter did was hand you the word the story was about. \textbf{ofrecer} unfolds into \emph{carry toward}.

The other three are plainer, and that is the honest proportion: some words open, some do not, and the only way to know is to try.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five words
  \item I lent my colleague the charger and he has not given it back
  \item I can offer you Thursday
  \item I have come to collect the order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To lend? (\textbf{prestar}.) To collect? (\textbf{recoger}.) What is hiding inside \emph{compañero}? (\textbf{pan}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(un aviso del curso) — read it as the person it is for}

\label{lesson:ES-C436-sintesis-aviso-grupo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el grupo} and \emph{recoger}. Both are in the notice you are about to read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read it once straight through, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{CURSO DE COCINA — AVISO} El \textbf{grupo} de los martes está completo. Podemos \textbf{ofrecer} plaza en el de los jueves. Los materiales se \textbf{recogen} en recepción el primer día.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which group is full
  \item what they can offer instead
  \item where and when you collect the materials
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Now produce it. Say aloud:

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I have changed to the Thursday group
  \item a colleague from work lent me the book
  \item I will collect the materials on the first day
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Notice what kind of text this is.} It is not a conversation, not a story and not a dialogue between two friends in a café. It is an administrative notice addressed to somebody who has to act on it — and that is what the A2 reading paper is mostly made of.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which group is full? (\textbf{el de los martes}.) What do they offer? (\textbf{plaza el jueves}.) What do you do with the materials? (\textbf{recogerlos en recepción}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
